notes: Claims counted per genre: tagline, place, date_range, description, debatable, 3 listen_for, 5 hallmarks, each link (label+reason as one), per artist dates/summary/2 contributions/recording/study prompt, each landmark recording. reacted_against is null on all 8 cards.
All 32 study prompts were checked mechanically: each is exactly the card's summary + contributions + recording, nothing added.

Null recording years (Toots '54-46', Colón 'El gran varón', Jobim 'Garota de Ipanema', Vinicius 'Samba da Benção', Fela 'Water No Get Enemy') are allowed by the writer brief where the corpus gives none; only Canção do Amor Demais has a year in the corpus.

2026 in the corpus but not on any card (no action unless used): T.I. 'twelfth and final album, Kill the King, was released in 2026'; Celia Cruz and Fela Kuti posthumous Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductions in 2026.

items.claim: Dramatic synthesized strings, brass and keys over a slow beat, often around 70 BPM felt in half-time.
items.note: Facts match ('typical trap beat is around 70 (140) BPM', 'often programmed in half-time'), but 'BPM' and 'felt in half-time' are unglossed jargon for a beginner.

fix.text: Dramatic synthesized strings, brass and keys over a beat that usually runs around 140 beats per minute but feels like a slow 70 (half-time).

items.claim: ...early trap rappers wrote about drug dealing and the struggle to get out.
items.note: Source: lyrics covered life in 'the trap', drug dealing 'and the struggle for success'. 'Struggle to get out' adds an escape narrative the source doesn't state.

fix.text: The name comes from Atlanta slang for a drug house, and early trap rappers wrote about life in the trap, drug dealing and the struggle for success. As one critic put it, in the early 2000s the trap was a real place, and the word was later used for music made about that place.

items.claim: Hard in the Paint (Waka Flocka Flame) (2010, song)
items.note: Not the artist's own record: it is Waka Flocka Flame's song, produced by Luger. The article does name it as notable ('Luger's first instrumental to hit the radio waves and became a hit by May 2010'), and the title credits Waka, so it is acceptable for a producer; flagged as asked.

items.claim: Where the word came from is unsettled: Toots Hibbert said it simply came out of his mouth while making 'Do the Reggay', historian Steve Barrow credits Clancy Eccles, and Bob Marley said it came from a Spanish term for 'the king's music'.
items.cited: genre sources (Infobox, intro, Origins and influences, Musical characteristics, Precursors, Emergence in Jamaica, International popularity, Cultural connections, Lyrical themes, Ska#intro)
items.note: Every part is true in the corpus, but only in Reggae#Etymology, which is not among the cited sections. Text is fine; the source list needs the Etymology section.

fix.text: Where the word came from is unsettled: Toots Hibbert said it simply came out of his mouth while making 'Do the Reggay', historian Steve Barrow credits Clancy Eccles, and Bob Marley said it came from a Spanish term for 'the king's music'.

items.claim: ...giving its relaxed, rocking phrasing. The intro to the Wailers' 'Stir It Up' is a textbook example of the guitar chop.
items.note: Source says the offbeat plus beat-three drum create 'a unique sense of phrasing' and 'An example is the intro to "Stir It Up"'. 'Relaxed, rocking' and 'textbook' are stronger than the source.

fix.text: Most pop leans on beat one; reggae accents the offbeats instead. Guitar or piano chops short chords between the counts while the drum stresses beat three, giving it a distinctive sense of phrasing. The intro to the Wailers' 'Stir It Up' is an example of the guitar chop.

items.claim: Scholar Michael Veal heard dub's reverb as a sonic metaphor for the African diaspora's experience of dislocation and memory.
items.note: Veal calls reverb a 'sonic metaphor for the condition of diaspora' and says echo and reverb 'elicit memories of African culture'. 'Dislocation' is not in the source.

fix.text: Delay units such as the Roland Space Echo, plus reverb and phasing, turn a song into a drifting soundscape. Scholar Michael Veal called dub's reverb a 'sonic metaphor for the condition of diaspora', used to call up memories of African culture.

items.claim: ...post-punk bands such as the Clash and Public Image Ltd took up its bass lines.
items.cited: Dub_music#Influence of dub on punk and rock music
items.note: Only Public Image Ltd is said to use dub-influenced bass lines. The Clash are described as collaborating with Lee Perry and Mikey Dread and covering 'Police & Thieves', not as taking up dub bass lines (and are a punk band in the source).

fix.text: In the 1970s the UK became a new centre of dub production, with Mad Professor among its best-known names. Punk and post-punk took it up: the Clash worked with Lee Perry and Mikey Dread, and Public Image Ltd used dub-influenced bass lines. Originators like Mad Professor and Lee Perry kept making dub into the 21st century.

sources.section: Influence of dub on punk and rock music

items.claim: grew_out_of out | dub's sense of space | The ambient article lists Jamaican dub among the sources ambient music drew on.
items.note: Ambient intro says ambient 'was presaged by ... Jamaican dub music', a weaker relation than 'sources ambient drew on'; 'sense of space' is not in the ambient source. (Dub_music#intro, not cited here, does say dub influenced ambient.)

fix.text: The ambient article names Jamaican dub among the styles that presaged ambient music, and the dub article lists ambient among the genres dub influenced.

items.claim: No Protection (Massive Attack v Mad Professor) (1995, album)
items.note: Named in his article ('In 1995 he produced No Protection'), but it is a dub remix of another act's album, jointly credited; not wholly his own record. An own-record alternative isn't named as notable in the cited sections (Dub Me Crazy series is, in Mad_Professor#Career, without a specific title).

items.claim: King Tubbys Meets Rockers Uptown (1976, album)
items.note: His own LP, but his article only lists it among 'a few LPs'; the notable item is the 1974 dub track (Rolling Stone's 266th greatest song). It is also near-identical to King Tubby's pick on the same card ('King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown', 1974, song), so a beginner gets the same title twice.

fix.text: King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown (1974, song) is already King Tubby's pick; for variety use 'East of the River Nile' (1971–1973 single for Aquarius), which his article names among his early recordings.

items.note: Latin America is supported (1970s section). 'To Africa' is true in the corpus but only in Salsa_music#African salsa (Fania All Stars in Kinshasa 1974, 'the largest wave of Cuban-based music to hit Africa was in the form of salsa'), which is not cited.

fix.text: (keep text) add source Salsa_music#African salsa

items.claim: The clave, a two-bar pattern often struck on two wooden sticks, that the other parts lock to.
items.note: Source: every instrument is 'either playing with the clave ... or playing independent of the clave rhythm (bass, maracas, güiro, cowbell)'. 'The other parts lock to' overstates it (the card's own hallmark2 gets it right). 'Two-bar' is not stated.

fix.text: The clave, a rhythm often struck on two wooden sticks, which the congas, timbales, piano and bongos play with.

items.claim: The 1964 album Getz/Gilberto set off a bossa nova craze in the US and beyond.
items.note: Cited genre sections only say Getz/Gilberto was Grammy-winning. Jobim#Career says its release 'created a bossa nova craze', but Astrud_Gilberto#The Girl from Ipanema says it was 'a major contributor to the already growing popularity of bossa nova beyond Brazil' (and Bossa_nova#History has the 1962 Carnegie Hall show and Quincy Jones's Big Band Bossa Nova). 'Set off' overstates.

fix.text: ...The 1964 album Getz/Gilberto, a major contributor to bossa nova's already growing popularity abroad, turned it into a craze in the US and beyond.

items.claim: She came to the Getz/Gilberto sessions as João's interpreter and was asked to sing the English lyrics; her whispery voice helped make the song a hit.
items.note: Hedge dropped: the source says 'Accounts vary as to exactly how Astrud was selected'; Ruy Castro says the idea was hers. 'Was asked' picks one account.

fix.text: She came to the Getz/Gilberto sessions as João's interpreter; accounts differ on whose idea it was, but she sang the English lyrics, and her whispery voice helped make the song a hit.

items.claim: From 1962 he sang new songs, including 'Garota de Ipanema', in small 'pocket shows' with Jobim and Gilberto in Rio.
items.note: Source: in August 1962 he first performed as a singer with Jobim and Gilberto; that was the first of his pocket shows; this phase ended in 1963. The card implies an ongoing series with both partners.

fix.text: In August 1962 he first sang on stage with Jobim and Gilberto in Rio, the first of his small 'pocket shows', where he presented new songs such as 'Garota de Ipanema'.

items.claim: ...He is widely regarded as one of the most important songwriters of the 20th century.
items.note: Sourced, but a ranking-style superlative (writer brief: no rankings). Low severity.

fix.text: A Brazilian composer, pianist and arranger known as Tom Jobim, considered one of the fathers of bossa nova for merging samba with cool jazz. Many of his songs became jazz standards.

items.claim: Drums that avoid the usual 2-and-4 backbeat, with tightly swung hi-hat triplets hinting at a clave.
items.note: Source: Allen 'makes sparing use' of the 2&4 backbeat (not 'avoids'); the hi-hat plays swung triplets, but it is the snare patterns that imply the clave. A listener would be pointed at the wrong drum.

fix.text: Drums that make sparing use of the usual 2-and-4 backbeat: tightly swung triplets on the hi-hat, and snare patterns that hint at a clave without stating it.

items.claim: ...from the late 1990s a Brooklyn scene led by Antibalas brought it to new listeners.
items.note: Source: 'a small Afrobeat scene began in Brooklyn, New York, with projects including Antibalas, The Daktaris and the Kokolo Afrobeat Orchestra'. 'Led by' ranks Antibalas over the others; 'brought it to new listeners' is said of 2000s DJs' compilations, not the Brooklyn scene.

fix.text: Fela's sons Femi and Seun carry the style on, and from the late 1990s a small Brooklyn scene grew, with bands such as Antibalas and the Daktaris. Its polyrhythms also reached Western music through Talking Heads' 1980 album Remain in Light.

items.claim: ...and took its name and form in Puerto Rico's 'underground' scene of the early 1990s.
items.note: The form took shape in the early-1990s underground scene, but the source says the name 'reggaeton' 'became prominent during the early 2000s' (it was coined in Puerto Rico; the music was called 'underground' and 'perreo' before). The sentence dates the name to the early 1990s.

fix.text: Reggaeton grew from the Spanish-language reggae of Panama, which traces back to Afro-Caribbean workers who came to build the canal, and took shape in Puerto Rico's 'underground' scene of the early 1990s; the name reggaeton, coined in Puerto Rico, became prominent in the early 2000s. ...

items.claim: In early records, cool vocals about isolation and city life; in 1980s hits, warmer songs about romance and escape.
items.note: Source describes early synth-pop as using 'droning electronics with little change in inflection' and lyrics about 'isolation, urban anomie' and emotional coldness; 'cool vocals' moves the description from the electronics to the singing, and the source says 1980s hits had 'emotional, at times operatic singers'.

fix.text: In early records, droning electronics and lyrics about isolation and city alienation; in 1980s hits, emotional, sometimes operatic singers and more optimistic songs about romance and escape.
